title: Psalm 3: David's Lament and Trust
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Firsts of Psalm 3
subpoints: First psalm with a title, indicating inspiration
First psalm ascribed to David
First of 13 psalms with historical context
First occurrence of the word Selah

outline.title: Historical Context: David's Flight
subpoints: David fled from Absalom's rebellion
Consequences of sin with Bathsheba and Uriah
Loss of kingdom and family turmoil
Parallel between David and Jesus as the Anointed

outline.title: Stanza 1: Lament Over Enemies
subpoints: Numerous enemies rising against David
Mockery that there is no help in God
Feeling of divine forsakenness
Connection to Psalm 22 and the Cross

outline.title: The Reality of Sin's Consequences
subpoints: Sin leads to the wilderness and turmoil
Forgiveness does not erase all temporal consequences
The greater grace of being dead unto sin
Loss of testimony and usefulness

outline.title: Intimacy with God
subpoints: David addresses God by the name Yahweh
The meaning of 'I AM' from Exodus
Covenant-keeping nature of God
Comparison to the New Testament 'Abba, Father'

summary:
In this sermon, Pastor Tito Lyro explores Psalm 3, highlighting its unique position as the first psalm with a title, the first ascribed to David, and the first to include the word 'Selah.' The psalm is situated within the historical narrative of David’s flight from his son Absalom, a crisis resulting from David’s earlier sin with Bathsheba. The pastor emphasizes that while God’s forgiveness is abundant, the temporal consequences of sin—such as family strife and loss of reputation—remain real, urging believers to pursue the grace of being dead to sin rather than relying solely on the grace of forgiveness.

The message draws a profound parallel between David’s experience and that of Jesus Christ, the ultimate Anointed One. Just as David felt forsaken by his own people, Jesus experienced the full weight of divine abandonment on the cross, as seen in Psalm 22. This connection allows believers to bring their own feelings of abandonment and discouragement to Christ, finding comfort in His shared experience.

Finally, the sermon addresses the intimacy of David’s relationship with God, noting how he addresses the Lord by His holy name, Yahweh ('I AM'). This reflects a deep covenantal trust that God will not forsake His people, mirroring the New Testament intimacy of calling God 'Abba, Father.' The sermon encourages the congregation to trust in God’s sustaining power despite the presence of numerous enemies and life’s trials.
